title: A Structural Approach to High-Frequency Event Studies: The Fed and Markets as Case History

p.t: A large literature offers competing explanations for why financial markets react so strongly to the announcements of central banks. The classic New Keynesian view is that surprise central bank communications proxy for shocks to a nominal interest rate rule of the type emphasized by Taylor (1993), which influence the real economy through an intertemporal substitution channel. More recent theories emphasize the effect of announcements on financial market risk premia (the risk premium channel), the information they impart about the state of the economy (the "Fed information shock" channel), or the role they play in revising the public's understanding of the central bank's reaction function and objectives (the perceived policy rule channel). Many questions about the interplay between central bank news and financial markets remain unanswered. A key challenge is that central bank announcements cover a wide-ranging set of themes, from interest rate policy, to forward guidance, to quantitative interventions, to the macroeconomic outlook. This plethora offers little reason to expect that the forces driving the reaction to one announcement resemble those driving another. What markets learn from Fed news is therefore an event-specific question, calling for a high-frequency event study that can allow for distinct theoretical channels across event-time. Yet existing event study approaches provide little to no announcement-specific evidence, and they offer limited insight into how and why market participants change their expectations in response to one event as compared to another. When prices jump on a piece of news, which primitive shocks did investors reassess, and how much did each revision contribute to the move?

Our first contribution is methodological: we integrate a high-frequency event study into a mixed-frequency macro-finance model and structural estimation. The resulting "mixedfrequency structural approach" to event study analysis allows us to address the question of why-as seen through the lens of a model-financial markets reacted to a given piece of news the way they did, effectively identifying state-dependent reaction functions to realworld events. The general approach can be applied in a wide variety of structural and semistructural settings whenever the research objective calls for a conceptual understanding of financial market responses to any type of news or event. 1In this article, we apply the approach to undertake a case study of the stock market's reactions to Federal Reserve (Fed) communications. Our structural estimation uses dozens of forward-looking series ranging from minutely financial market data to biannual survey forecast data. These data, along with the model and structural estimation, allow us to infer jumps in investor beliefs about the latent state of the economy, the perceived sources of primitive economic risk driving that state, and the future conduct of monetary policy, all in response to Fed news. In turn, movements in these beliefs generate endogenous movements in subjective risk premia. The theoretical framework is a two-agent asset pricing model with New Keynesian style macroeconomic dynamics in which the two agents have heterogeneous beliefs, as in Bianchi, Lettau, and Ludvigson (2022) (BLL hereafter). One agent is a representative "investor" who is forward-looking, reacts swiftly to news, and earns income solely from investments in the stock market and a one-period nominal bond. Macroeconomic dynamics are specified by a set of equations similar to those in New Keynesian models, and can be thought of as driven by a representative "household/worker" that supplies labor, has access to the nominal bond, but holds no stock market wealth. Unlike investors, the household/worker forms expectations in a backward-looking manner using adaptive learning rules, consistent with survey evidence on how households actually arrive at their beliefs (Malmendier and Nagel (2016), Coibion, Gorodnichenko, Kumar, and Pedemonte (2020)). In the model, the conduct of monetary policy may undergo nonrecurrent regime shifts, or "structural breaks," in the parameters of a nominal interest rate rule. Such regime changes give rise to endogenously long-lasting changes in real interest rates that are conceptually distinct from those generated by a monetary policy shock, an innovation in the nominal rate that is uncorrelated with inflation, economic growth, and shifts in the policy rule parameters.

With this feature at hand, we explicitly model investor beliefs about future regime change. Investors monitor central bank communications for information that would lead them to revise the perceived probability of transitioning out of the current policy regime into a perceived "Alternative regime" they believe will come next. They also understand that new information may change their minds in the future, and take that into account when forming expectations. A Fed announcement is therefore a bona fide news shock, one to which investors may react by revising their nowcasts and forecasts of the current and future economic state, their beliefs about the future conduct of monetary policy, and their perceptions of financial market risk. These revisions are what our estimation measures. Because the model lets beliefs about the economic state move with the news, we can measure directly how much of the market volatility around announcements is attributable to "Fed information shocks". Beliefs about the economic state and about future policy are both disciplined by the data: we map numerous forward-looking variables-multiple surveys of expectations together with financial market indicators from spot and futures markets-onto model-implied equations for investor beliefs, estimating all parameters and latent states. Our second contribution concerns how these beliefs are transmitted to asset prices. In a simplified version of the model that admits a closed-form solution, we show that the subjective risk premium decomposes into two economically distinct channels, plus two terms that are quantitatively negligible under plausible calibrations. The first is a macro volatility channel: when investors expect the central bank to stabilize economic growth more aggressively, cash-flow growth becomes less volatile, lowering the quantity of risk borne by equity holders. The second is a Fed put channel: that same expectation implies a lower discount rate precisely when cash-flow growth weakens, providing insurance to equity holders and putting a floor under stock prices. Proposition 1 establishes that when investors attach a higher probability to moving to a rule that is more activist on output growth, both terms fall, so that the two channels reinforce one another. They do so, however, for different reasons. The macro volatility channel operates only to the extent that policy can actually stabilize real activity, which depends on the sensitivity of output to the real interest rate; the Fed put channel is instead strongest when that sensitivity is low. The Fed put channel thus implies that monetary policy can exert an influence on risk premia even when it has little capacity to stabilize the real economy.

The two channels play different roles. Macro volatility is the dominant contributor to the level of the premium, since a more volatile economy raises the compensation investors require to hold equity. The Fed put enters with the opposite sign, as insurance, and is smaller in absolute value. But it is the Fed put that drives the premium as beliefs about the next policy rule shift: estimating the full model, we find that it accounts for the majority of the beliefdriven movement in premia in each of the three policy regimes we estimate, and accounts for a rising share over time, from 55% to 73%. These movements are driven almost entirely by beliefs about future activism on economic growth rather than on inflation: holding the perceived inflation response fixed across the current and Alternative rules leaves the results essentially unchanged. These empirical findings suggest that market risk premia respond to monetary policy for reasons that extend beyond its consequences for macroeconomic stability, and are consistent with a Fed that has limited ability to prevent recessions but considerable ability to stabilize financial markets. Turning to individual announcements, the structural estimation implies that investors seldom learn only about conventional monetary policy shocks from central bank commu-nications. Instead, jumps in financial market variables in response to central bank communications are caused by a mix of context-specific forces, whose relative importance the methodology quantifies event by event. On January 3, 2001, for example, the Fed surprised markets by reducing its target for the federal funds rate (FFR) by 50 basis points, and the stock market vaulted 4.2% in the 30-minute window surrounding the announcement. Yet our estimates imply that investors' perception of an accommodative policy shock to the short rate played only a small first-order role in the surge. The most quantitatively important contributors were instead a downward revision in investor expectations of financial market liquidity premia and an upward revision in expectations of corporate earnings as a share of aggregate output, revisions identified in the data by jumps in credit spreads and in professional survey nowcasts of S&P 500 earnings measured immediately before and after the policy announcement. This event can be contrasted with the FOMC announcement of April 18, 2001, in which the market rose 2.5% after the Greenspan Fed again surprised the stock market with a 50 basis point reduction in the funds rate. In this case the biggest estimated driver was a change in investor beliefs about how monetary policy would be conducted in the future: markets priced in a higher likelihood that the Fed would soon shift its policy rule toward one that more aggressively stabilized output fluctuations, thereby strengthening the Fed put and lowering subjective risk premia on impact. This shift in beliefs is identified in the data by jumps in both the stock market and in Fed funds futures rates that cannot be explained by rolling forward the current policy rule.

A further set of results pertains to the role of "Fed information shocks." Following Jarocinski and Karadi (2020), we define an event with a Fed information shock as one that features a positive comovement between short-term interest rates and the stock market within a narrow window around a policy announcement. We find that the most quantitatively important announcements of this type, measured by how much the stock market responded, are difficult to reconcile with standard notions of a Fed information shock. On October 29, 2008, for example, the Fed announced that it would lower its target for the FFR by 50 basis points to 1%, while the stock market fell 2% in the 30 minutes surrounding the announcement. According to our estimates, the market declined not because investors learned new negative information about the economic outlook. If anything, perceptions about the economic state were revised favorably, suggesting that investors believed the rate cut would at least help to support the economy. We find instead that these reasons for optimism were more than offset by a sharp downgrade in the perceived likelihood that policy would soon shift toward a rule more responsive to economic growth. The cut left the funds rate at 1% in the midst of the worst financial crisis in a century, bringing the effective lower bound into view. The shift in beliefs about future policy around this announcement suggests that the Fed was seen as incapable of delivering a stronger conventional policy response to faltering growth. The announcement therefore weakened the perceived Fed put and raised subjective risk premia, pushing stocks down even as rates fell.

Related Literature The research in this paper connects with a large and growing body of evidence that the values of long-term financial assets and expected return premia respond sharply to the announcements of central banks. 2 A classic assumption of this literature is that high-frequency financial market reactions to Fed announcements proxy for conventional monetary policy "shocks," i.e., innovations in a Taylor (1993)-type nominal interest rate rule. By contrast, Jarocinski and Karadi (2020), Cieslak and Schrimpf (2019), and Hillenbrand (2021) argue that some of the fluctuations are likely driven by the revelation of information by the Fed, a "Fed information effect" channel emphasized in earlier work by Romer and Romer (2000), Campbell, Evans, Fisher, and Justiniano (2012), Melosi (2017), and Nakamura and Steinsson (2018). Related, Cieslak and Pang (2021) identify monetary, growth, and risk premium shocks from Fed news using sign-restricted VARs, Bauer and Swanson (2023) argue that markets are surprised by the Fed's response to recent economic events, and Bauer, Pflueger, and Sundaram (2022) use survey data to estimate perceived policy rules, finding that they are subject to substantial time-variation. The mixed-frequency structural approach proposed here extends these literatures by allowing for announcement-specific results seen through the lens of a structural asset pricing model, and by providing evidence that expected return premia vary, in part, because the perceived quantity of stock market risk fluctuates around policy announcements due to changing beliefs about future monetary policy conduct.

Our work also relates to a theoretical literature focused on the implications of monetary policy for asset prices going back to Piazzesi (2005). Kekre and Lenel (2021) and Pflueger and Rinaldi (2020) develop carefully calibrated theoretical models that imply stock market return premia vary in response to a monetary policy shock. These theories use different mechanisms but are all silent on the possible role of Fed announcement effects or of changing policy rules in driving market fluctuations, features that are at the heart of our analysis. Our structural estimates are consistent with the interpretation of Cieslak and Vissing-Jorgensen (2021) based on textual analyses of FOMC documents, and indicate that subjective risk premia vary with beliefs about the strength of a Fed put on the stock market. The two-agent structural model of this paper builds on BLL, who focus on the low frequency implications for asset valuations of changes in the conduct of monetary policy. Our methodological advance over BLL, and to the best of our knowledge over the extant literature, is to provide theoretical insight into why markets respond to news, including estimates of revisions in investor beliefs about future monetary policy in the minutes surrounding Fed announcements. We show how forward-looking variables, such as survey expectations and asset prices, can be used both to estimate the market's perceived probability of a near-term policy regime change and to extract beliefs about the nature of the regime that will follow. BLL, and more recently Nagel (2024), underscore the importance of adopting empirical realism in the modeling of household inflation expectations for studying how monetary policy affects financial markets. Extensive evidence from survey microdata shows that households do not form expectations rationally according to the rules assumed by classic New Keynesian models. Instead, that evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that monetary policy must pursue large and persistent changes in real rates in order to counter inertia in household expectations that-unlike markets-are relatively impervious to Fed announcements. Such persistent monetary non-neutrality rationalizes why markets for ultra long-duration assets like stocks pay so much attention to Fed announcements in the first place.

In contemporaneous work, Caballero and Simsek (2022) study a two-agent, "two-speed" economy with investors and households similar in spirit to BLL. Their purely theoretical investigation studies the relation between Fed policy and a broad-based financial conditions index, allowing for two-way feedback between financial conditions and the economy. Our work is an empirical complement that estimates the high-frequency impact of Fed news on the stock market. Our use of mixed-frequency data also differs in purpose from a pre-existing reduced-form forecasting literature that combines frequencies in state space models in order to augment lower frequency prediction models with more timely high-frequency data (e.g., Giannone, Reichlin, and Small (2008), Ghysels and Wright (2009), Schorfheide and Song (2015)). We use high-frequency, forward-looking data available within the decision interval to infer revisions in the intraperiod beliefs of investors about the economic state to be realized at the end of the decision interval. This allows us to treat Fed announcements as bona fide news shocks, as perceived by investors, rather than as ultra high-frequency macro shocks that happen to occur around Fed communications. Finally, this paper contributes to the literature on changes in the conduct of monetary pol-icy. Early contributions employed VAR models with either recursively estimated, smoothly time-varying parameters (e.g., Cogley and Sargent (2005), Primiceri (2005), Boivin (2006), and Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2011)) or regime-switching specifications (e.g., Sims and Zha (2006)), while more recent studies have modeled regime changes within DSGE frameworks (e.g., Bianchi (2013), Bianchi and Ilut (2017), Bianchi and Melosi (2017), and Liu, Waggoner, and Zha (2011)), or used survey data to estimate perceived rules (Bauer, Pflueger, and Sundaram (2022)). This paper innovates along two dimensions. First, we allow for nonrecurrent regime changes and use forward-looking variables to infer a time-varying perceived probability of regime shifts in the policy rule. Second, we use a structural model to interpret discontinuous movements in these variables around FOMC announcements. Our focus on beliefs about future policy regimes via a perceived Alternative policy rule compliments this work. Estimates of time-varying or drifting rules characterize the rule in place at each date, which is what the transmission of policy to inflation and output requires. Equity valuation makes a different demand: a long-duration claim depends on the rule investors expect to prevail over its life, not on the rule in force today. Appendix I bears this out: allowing investors to update their understanding of the current rule after an announcement, even by sizable amounts, leaves our stock market results essentially unchanged, whereas revisions in beliefs about the next rule move prices substantially. Modeling how those beliefs evolve is therefore essential for the asset pricing questions we ask. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents preliminary empirical evidence that we use to pin down the timing of monetary regime changes in our sample. Section 3 describes the mixed-frequency structural macro-finance model and equilibrium solution. Section 4 develops a simplified version of the model that admits a closed-form solution and isolates the channels through which beliefs about policy activism affect risk premia. Section 5 describes the structural estimation and the mixed-frequency filtering algorithm. Section 6 presents our empirical findings. Section 7 concludes. A large amount of additional material on the model, estimation, and data has been placed in an Online Appendix.

In the structural model of the next section, investors form beliefs about future regime change in the conduct of monetary policy. We therefore begin with preliminary evidence of infrequent, sizable shifts in the conduct of policy over the course of our sample. Break dates, if any, are freely estimated and dictated by the data. Figure I panel (a) plots the real federal funds rate r t , measured here as the nominal rate minus expected inflation, proxied by a four-quarter moving average of realized inflation. Panel (b) plots the difference between this rate and an estimate of the neutral rate of interest r * t from Laubach and Williams (2003), effectively a low-frequency component of the real funds rate. We refer to this spread as the monetary policy spread and denote its time t value by mps t . The mps t may be considered a crude measure of the stance of monetary policy, that is, of whether policy is accommodative or restrictive. We allow for the possibility of infrequent regime changes in the means of r t and mps t , governed by a discrete-valued latent state variable ξ P t that is presumed to follow an N Pstate nonrecurrent regime-switching Markov process, i.e., structural breaks. A regime shift therefore need not move to a regime that is identically equal to one in the past, an event that has probability zero, though it may be arbitrarily close to one. This specification is both more plausible and more flexible than recurrent regime switching, which restricts new regimes to repeat old ones exactly. 3Figure I reports the results for the case of two structural breaks (N P = 3), estimated separately for r t and mps t . The estimated break dates are identical across the two series, and thus so are the regime subperiods. The chosen r * t measure therefore has no influence on the estimated break dates, though it remains useful for gauging the persistence of swings in r t around its low-frequency component.

The breaks we identify are decades long, consistent with an earlier literature documenting that monetary regime changes are infrequent (Clarida, Gali, and Gertler (2000); Lubik and Schorfheide (2004); Sims and Zha (2006); Bianchi (2013)). The first subperiod, 1961:Q1 to 1978:Q3, is one in which r t was low and mps t persistently negative. This "Great Inflation" regime coincides with a run-up in inflation and with two oil shocks in the 1970s that were arguably exacerbated by a Fed that failed to react sufficiently proactively. A second, "Great Moderation" regime begins in 1978:Q4, when a structural break drove upward jumps in both r t and mps t . This period of more restrictive monetary policy lasted through 2001:Q3 and covers the Volcker disinflation and the moderation in economic volatility that followed. The third, "Post Millennial" regime spans 2001:Q4 to 2020:Q1 and represents a new prolonged period of low real interest rates. It begins shortly after the inception of public narratives on the "Greenspan Put," the perceived attempt of Chair Greenspan to prop up securities markets in the wake of the IT bust, a recession, and the aftermath of 9/11, by lowering interest rates. It continues with the explicit "low-for-long" forward guidance policies under Chair Bernanke that repeatedly promised over several years to keep interest rates at ultra low levels for an extended period of time. Below we refer to these three regimes in abbreviated terms as the GI, GM, and PM regimes.

The preliminary evidence of this section is used to set the timing of possible policy regime changes in the structural model. 4 To accomplish this, we set the break dates for regime changes in the model's policy rule to coincide with the regime sequence for ξ P t displayed in Figure I. It should be emphasized, however, that all regime-dependent parameters of the policy rule are freely estimated under symmetric priors, and so are treated as equally likely to increase or decrease across the regime subperiods, if they change at all. We use Bayesian model comparison of estimated structural models that differ according to the number of policy regimes to decide on the appropriate number, and find that N P = 3 works well. Our structural estimation therefore spans three different policy regimes across the GI, GM, and PM subperiods shown in Figure I.

p.s: Investor Beliefs About Future Monetary Policy
p.t: To model the uncertainty investors face about the conduct of monetary policy, we assume that they expect the policy rule to be subject to infrequent, nonrecurrent regime changes, and that they can accurately estimate the rule currently in place. The latter assumption is a reasonable approximation for stock market dynamics, for two reasons. First, uncertainty about the current rule alone, holding fixed beliefs about future policy, is unlikely to matter much for a long duration asset, because what matters for such assets is not where the policy rule is today but where it will be for the foreseeable future. Since investors in our specification continuously update their beliefs about the probability of moving to a new policy regime as soon as the beginning of the next month, additional uncertainty about the current rule is relatively unimportant. Appendix I of the Online Appendix confirms this: the stock market results reported below are virtually unchanged when investors are allowed to update their understanding of the current rule after an announcement, even by sizable amounts, in contrast to the large effects of changing beliefs about where policy will settle. Second, the Fed's observed practice is to telegraph an intentional change in the stance of policy clearly, but to be comparatively vague about how long that change will last and what will come afterwards. Investors scrutinize Fed communications not because they are most interested in what the central bank is doing today, but because they must contemplate a future in which it could operate differently from today, or from any regime that has come before.

p.t: To model these circumstances, we assume that for each time t policy regime indexed by ξ P t , investors hold in their minds a perceived "Alternative policy rule" indexed by ξ A t that they believe will come next, whenever the current policy regime ends: Investors do not have perfect foresight: the regime that replaces the current one will never be exactly as previously imagined. When a regime ends, investors update their understanding of the new current policy rule and proceed to contemplate a new perceived Alternative for the rule after that. Investors form beliefs not only about what the next policy rule will look like, but also continuously assess the likelihood of switching to ξ A t by the beginning of next period. Specifically, for each ξ P t they hold beliefs about the probability of remaining in ξ P t versus changing to ξ A t next month, but do not consider anything after that. This last aspect is a form of bounded rationality that is arguably plausible in the context of infrequent regime changes. In the nonrecurrent setup of the model it implies that the pondered Alternative is treated as an absorbing state as of time t, since the probability of returning to any previous rule is zero by definition. We formalize these ideas with a belief regime sequence governed by a discrete-valued variable ξ b t ∈ {1, 2, ...B, B + 1} with B + 1 states. The regimes ξ b t = 1, 2, ...B represent a grid of perceived probabilities that the current policy rule will still be in place next period, ordered so that ξ b t = 1 is the lowest such probability and ξ b t = B the highest. The regime ξ b t = B + 1 captures the perceived probability of staying in the Alternative regime once it is reached. The perceived regimes are modeled with a transition matrix taking the form

Investor Information and Updating Let I t denote the time t information set of investors, which includes the current policy regime ξ P t , their perceived Alternative regime ξ A t , their beliefs about monetary policy ξ b t , and additional data available at mixed frequencies that we do not explicitly specify. Investors observe S t and consume payout at a monthly frequency, but price assets continuously by revising expectations in response to news. With S t observed only at the end of the month, any Fed news that the investor attends to within a month results in the updating of a nowcast of S t , which we assume they produce by filtering a potentially extensive database of timely, high-frequency information in I t . This database is unobserved by the econometrician, but our estimation will not rely on it, as explained below. Investors therefore use I t in two ways. First, given a baseline monthly decision interval, they update their previous nowcasts and subjective expectations once S t is observed at the end of every t. Second, they allocate attention to updating nowcasts of S t and beliefs ξ b t about future monetary policy at specific times within a month when the central bank releases information. This higher-frequency attentiveness echoes real-world "Fed watching" and is the mechanism through which the model accommodates swift market reactions to surprise central bank announcements, driving jumps in investor perceptions of stock market risk

To estimate how an investor in the model would react to news, we undertake a high-frequency event study using narrow (30 minute) windows around a news event. What distinguishes our approach from common event study analyses is that we study reactions to specific events as they would be understood through the lens of a structural model. News generates a set of signals about the current economic state S t with varying degrees of precision. An FOMC statement announcing a change in the target federal funds rate, for instance, is a signal with infinite precision, because it removes all uncertainty about the end-of-month target funds rate. By contrast, announcements that speak to the macroeconomic outlook are signals with considerable noise, because the Fed cannot directly control the outcome. In either case we are interested in measuring the jump in investor expectations attributable to the news per se. To do so, we design a filter that infers real-time updating of expectations about the current economic state S t , to be revealed at the end of the period, in response to news events occurring within the period. Since these represent expectations for the current period, we refer to them as nowcasts. Data and Measurement Our full dataset spans January 1961 through February 2020. The sample of Fed news consists of 220 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) press releases covering February 4th, 1994 to January 29th, 2020. Observations on most series are available monthly; for quarterly GDP growth we interpolate to monthly frequency using the method in Stock and Watson (2010). An explicit description of the mapping between our observables and their model counterparts, and a complete description of each data series and its sources, is given in Appendix B of the Online Appendix. We use high-frequency pre-and post-FOMC observations on the following variables: daily survey expectations of inflation, GDP growth, and S&P 500 earnings from Bloomberg (BBG); daily observations on the spread between the 20-year Baa rate and the 20-year Treasury bond rate (Baa spread hereafter); minutely observations on four distinct federal funds futures (FFF) contract rates with different expiries; and minutely observations on the S&P 500 market value. These data serve two purposes. First, they allow us to measure the effect of Fed news on investor beliefs and perceptions in tight windows around announcements. Second, the timely information they contain allows us to account for economic news that predated the FOMC announcement but arrived after the latest observations on stale monthly survey data (Bauer and Swanson (2023)). By conditioning on close-range, pre-and postannouncement observations for inflation, GDP growth, and earnings expectations, as well as credit spreads (at daily frequency), interest rate futures, and the stock market (10 minutes before and 20 minutes after), we ensure that our estimated post-announcement jumps in nowcasts cannot be readily attributed to stale economic news.

At lower frequencies, we use the household-level Survey of Consumers (SOC) from the University of Michigan to discipline household expectations, and three professional forecaster surveys, from Bluechip (BC), the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF), and Livingston (LIV), to discipline investor expectations. We measure investor expectations at multiple horizons using the four professional surveys, treating each as a noisy signal on the true underlying investor expectations process. A number of series are used because they have obvious model counterparts. Data for Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth and inflation are mapped into the model implications for output growth and inflation; data on the current effective federal funds rate (FFR) are mapped into the model's implications for the current nominal interest rate; and data on the FFF market and the BC survey measure of the expected FFR 12 months ahead are mapped into the model's implications for investor expectations of the FFR. 14 Data on long-dated FFF contracts and survey forecasts of the funds rate a year or more out are especially helpful for identifying the parameters of the Alternative policy rule, since investors' longer-term forecasts are dominated by where they believe future policy will be rather than by the rule currently in place. We discipline the earnings share of output K t with observations on the ratio of S&P 500 earnings to GDP, accounting for the fact that earnings in the data differ from the payout shareholders actually receive by allowing for observation error in the relevant observation equation. Finally, data on the Baa spread are mapped into the model's implications for the liquidity premium lp t , a catchall for factors outside the model that could affect the subjective equity premium, including changes in the perceived liquidity and safety attributes of Treasuries, default risk, flights to quality, and sentiment. We use the Baa spread as an observable likely to be correlated with many of these factors, but our measurement equation allows for both a constant and a slope coefficient on the spread, along with observation error, in order to soak up variation in this latent variable that may not move identically with the spread.

This section presents results from the structural estimation based on the modal values of the posterior distribution for the parameters. The estimated credible sets indicate that the parameters are tightly identified, and we report other moments of the posterior in Table A.1 of the Online Appendix. For all five events, the largest share of the variation in pd t is attributable to movements in the subjective equity premium. The announcement of October 29, 2008 is associated with the largest absolute decline in the perceived probability of monetary regime change, as shown in panel (a): the perceived probability that the central bank would soon transition to an Alternative rule featuring more aggressive stabilization of the real economy falls sharply. Such a belief dashes hopes for a stronger Fed put, since it means the central bank is less likely to engineer a lower discount rate when cash flows are expected to grow more slowly. The result is a large rise in pdv t (r ex ) and a correspondingly large fall in pd t . Notably, this rise occurs despite the downward revision in the liquidity premium at the same announcement documented above, which by itself would have pushed pdv t (r ex ) lower. The belief-driven subjective risk premium component was therefore large enough to reverse the sign of the total, an event-level counterpart to the dominance of the Fed put channel in Figure V. Conversely, the March 11, 2008 announcement of an expansion of securities lending through the TSLF is the event associated with the largest increase in the perceived probability of exiting the current policy rule over the next 12 months, and is the mirror image of October 29, 2008. The stock market rose around this announcement, and panel (b) shows that the most important contributor was a decline in the subjective equity premium driven by a lower perceived quantity of risk in the stock market. The announcement of new lending facilities to support the economy amid a financial crisis evidently raised the perceived probability of shifting to a policy regime characterized by more aggressive stabilization of economic growth. The Fed put flavor of this event shows how Fed news can move markets by altering beliefs about future policies to limit downside risk, immediately changing risk premia.

What do financial markets learn from news? We develop a methodology to address this question, using the stock market's reaction to Fed announcements as a case study, by integrating a high-frequency event study into a mixed-frequency macro-finance model and structural estimation. Allowing investor beliefs to jump at announcements yields granular evidence on why markets react as they do. We also show how to model expectations in the presence of structural breaks, and how forward-looking data can be used to infer what agents expect from the next policy regime. The approach applies in a variety of other settings in which news moves prices. Why are markets so responsive to central bank communications? We find a mix of context-specific forces: revisions in beliefs about the latent economic state, including the corporate earnings share of output and credit spreads, and revisions in beliefs about the future conduct of policy. The latter operate chiefly through the perceived quantity of stock market risk, and we show that they do so through two channels: macro volatility and a Fed put. Macro volatility governs the level of the premium; the Fed put-insurance that enters with the opposite sign-dominates how the premium moves as beliefs about the next rule shift, accounting for most of that movement in every regime. The high-frequency decompositions agree: announcement-day movements in the price-payout ratio are driven primarily by subjective risk premia, not by expected cash flows or real rates. Because such belief shifts move stock prices and short rates in the same direction, they also generate the comovement often read as evidence of Fed information shocks.

Figure A.II shows a decomposition that is analogous to that in Figure VIII for the top four FOMC announcements in terms of absolute jumps in the market. Each panel plots the shock decomposition for one announcement. The first bar labeled "base" shows the results for our baseline model, which repeats information from Figure (VIII). The next three bars show what would happen if investors had-in contrast to our baseline model-updated beliefs about the current policy rule in the wake of the announcement. Specifically, we assume they update their belief about the activism coefficient on output growth, ψ y as a result of the announcement. In these cases investors' pre-announcement belief is equal to the true ψ y , but the post-announcement belief changes to some ψ * y ̸ = ψ y . The plot shows different cases where ψ * y = 0.5ψ y , 1.5ψ y , 2ψ y . The red triangles show the jump in the market implied by each specification, while the black dot shows the jump in the data. For the baseline model results shown in the first bars, the black dots and red triangles coincide. For the other specifications, the differences show the result of allowing investors to update their assessment of the current policy rule as a result of the announcement. We can see that the differences are negligible: the difference between the baseline model (black dot) and the red triangles in each case are small. Moreover, the relative contribution of different perceived shocks is virtually unchanged from the baseline case. In particular, changing perceptions about the economic state and/or beliefs about future regime change remain important contributors to the market's jump in all cases.
